front_blocks.md: Define **nuclear fission**.

back_blocks.md: **Nuclear fission** is when one large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei.

front_blocks.md: What are the three sources of **nuclear energy**?

back_blocks.md: **Nuclear fusion**, **nuclear fission** and **radioactive decay**.

cards.front_md: What are the three sources of **nuclear energy**?

front_blocks.md: What nucleus is formed when **deuterium** and **tritium** nuclei fuse, and what else is released?

back_blocks.md: A **helium** nucleus is formed, with the release of energy.

cards.front_md: What nucleus is formed when **deuterium** and **tritium** nuclei fuse, and what else is released?

front_blocks.md: The energy from 1 kg of hydrogen that undergoes fusion is equivalent to the energy from burning about **______** of coal.

back_blocks.md: The energy from 1 kg of hydrogen that undergoes fusion is equivalent to the energy from burning about **10 million kilograms** of coal.

front_blocks.md: In nuclear fission, what are the **parent nucleus** and **daughter nuclei**?

back_blocks.md: The **parent nucleus** is the large nucleus that splits; the **daughter nuclei** are the smaller nuclei that are produced.

cards.front_md: In nuclear fission, what are the **parent nucleus** and **daughter nuclei**?
cards.back_md: The **parent nucleus** is the large nucleus that splits; the **daughter nuclei** are the smaller nuclei that are produced.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Nuclear fusion occurs naturally on Earth.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Nuclear fusion does **not** happen naturally on Earth; it occurs naturally in **stars**, although fusion reactors are currently in development on Earth.

front_blocks.md: Define **nuclear fission**.

back_blocks.md: **Nuclear fission** is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei.

cards.front_md: Define **nuclear fission**.
cards.back_md: **Nuclear fission** is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei.

front_blocks.md: Define a **fissile material**.

back_blocks.md: A **fissile material** (such as certain isotopes of uranium and plutonium) can undergo fission under the right conditions, making it suitable as a fuel in nuclear power stations.

cards.front_md: Define a **fissile material**.
cards.back_md: A **fissile material** (such as certain isotopes of uranium and plutonium) can undergo fission under the right conditions, making it suitable as a fuel in nuclear power stations.

front_blocks.md: What is the difference between **spontaneous** and **induced** fission?

back_blocks.md: In **spontaneous fission**, an unstable nucleus splits without extra energy being added. In **induced fission**, the nucleus first absorbs a **neutron**, which makes it unstable enough to decay almost immediately.

cards.front_md: What is the difference between **spontaneous** and **induced** fission?
cards.back_md: In **spontaneous fission**, an unstable nucleus splits without extra energy being added. In **induced fission**, the nucleus first absorbs a **neutron**, which makes it unstable enough to decay almost immediately.

front_blocks.md: Why must the fission of uranium-235 be **induced** rather than left to occur spontaneously?

back_blocks.md: Uranium-235 has a very long half-life (700 million years), so it has low activity and releases energy too slowly to be useful in a nuclear power station.

cards.front_md: Why must the fission of uranium-235 be **induced** rather than left to occur spontaneously?
cards.back_md: Uranium-235 has a very long half-life (700 million years), so it has low activity and releases energy too slowly to be useful in a nuclear power station.

front_blocks.md: When a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, it becomes uranium-236, which is very **______** and splits almost immediately by nuclear fission.

back_blocks.md: When a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, it becomes uranium-236, which is very **unstable** and splits almost immediately by nuclear fission.

cards.front_md: When a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, it becomes uranium-236, which is very **______** and splits almost immediately by nuclear fission.
cards.back_md: When a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, it becomes uranium-236, which is very **unstable** and splits almost immediately by nuclear fission.

front_blocks.md: What three things are produced when a uranium-235 nucleus undergoes induced fission?

back_blocks.md: Two smaller **daughter nuclei**, two or three **neutrons**, and **gamma rays**.

cards.front_md: What three things are produced when a uranium-235 nucleus undergoes induced fission?
cards.back_md: Two smaller **daughter nuclei**, two or three **neutrons**, and **gamma rays**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In fission, energy is transferred from the nuclear potential energy of the original nucleus into the kinetic energy of the products.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
This kinetic energy of the fast-moving fission products can be harnessed and converted into **electrical energy** in a nuclear power station.

cards.back_md:

front_blocks.md: Define a **chain reaction**.

back_blocks.md: A **chain reaction** occurs when a neutron emitted from the splitting of a nucleus causes further nuclei to split, and the neutrons emitted from these cause further fission reactions.

cards.front_md: Define a **chain reaction**.
cards.back_md: A **chain reaction** occurs when a neutron emitted from the splitting of a nucleus causes further nuclei to split, and the neutrons emitted from these cause further fission reactions.

front_blocks.md: Define **critical mass**.

back_blocks.md: The **critical mass** is the minimum mass of fissile material required for a chain reaction to be maintained.

cards.front_md: Define **critical mass**.
cards.back_md: The **critical mass** is the minimum mass of fissile material required for a chain reaction to be maintained.

front_blocks.md: What is the purpose of the **control rods** in a nuclear reactor?

back_blocks.md: To **absorb neutrons**. Lowering the rods further **decreases** the rate of fission (more neutrons absorbed); raising the rods **increases** the rate of fission (fewer neutrons absorbed).

cards.front_md: What is the purpose of the **control rods** in a nuclear reactor?
cards.back_md: To **absorb neutrons**. Lowering the rods further **decreases** the rate of fission (more neutrons absorbed); raising the rods **increases** the rate of fission (fewer neutrons absorbed).

front_blocks.md: What is the purpose of the **moderator** in a nuclear reactor?

back_blocks.md: To **slow down** the fast-moving neutrons produced by fission, so they reach **thermal equilibrium** with the moderator, becoming **thermal neutrons** that can react efficiently with the uranium fuel.

cards.front_md: What is the purpose of the **moderator** in a nuclear reactor?
cards.back_md: To **slow down** the fast-moving neutrons produced by fission, so they reach **thermal equilibrium** with the moderator, becoming **thermal neutrons** that can react efficiently with the uranium fuel.

front_blocks.md: What is the purpose of the **shielding** around a nuclear reactor, and what is it made from?

back_blocks.md: To **absorb hazardous radiation** emitted by the daughter nuclei and neutrons produced during fission. It is made from a wall of **steel** and **concrete**, nearly 2 metres thick.

cards.front_md: What is the purpose of the **shielding** around a nuclear reactor, and what is it made from?
cards.back_md: To **absorb hazardous radiation** emitted by the daughter nuclei and neutrons produced during fission. It is made from a wall of **steel** and **concrete**, nearly 2 metres thick.

front_blocks.md: If the mass of fissile material exceeds the **______**, the rate of reaction accelerates, which can cause a huge, uncontrolled release of energy.

back_blocks.md: If the mass of fissile material exceeds the **critical mass**, the rate of reaction accelerates, which can cause a huge, uncontrolled release of energy.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Lowering the control rods further into a nuclear reactor increases the rate of fission.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Lowering the control rods further **decreases** the rate of fission, because more neutrons are absorbed.

front_blocks.md: Define **nuclear fusion**.

back_blocks.md: **Nuclear fusion** is when two light nuclei join together to form a heavier nucleus.

cards.front_md: Define **nuclear fusion**.
cards.back_md: **Nuclear fusion** is when two light nuclei join together to form a heavier nucleus.

front_blocks.md: Define the **fuel** required for nuclear fusion.

back_blocks.md: Isotopes of **hydrogen**, which are found in water.

cards.front_md: Define the **fuel** required for nuclear fusion.

front_blocks.md: Why has nuclear fusion proven very hard to reproduce on Earth?

back_blocks.md: It requires extremely **high temperatures** to maintain, which are very difficult to achieve and sustain outside of stars.

cards.front_md: Why has nuclear fusion proven very hard to reproduce on Earth?
cards.back_md: It requires extremely **high temperatures** to maintain, which are very difficult to achieve and sustain outside of stars.

front_blocks.md: Where does the energy released during nuclear fusion come from?

back_blocks.md: A very small amount of the reacting particles' **mass** is converted into energy.

cards.front_md: Where does the energy released during nuclear fusion come from?
cards.back_md: A very small amount of the reacting particles' **mass** is converted into energy.

front_blocks.md: Give three advantages of fusion reactors over fission reactors.

back_blocks.md: Fusion generates **more energy** than fission per kilogram of fuel, the fuel (hydrogen isotopes from water) is **more abundant** than uranium or plutonium, and fusion produces **no long-lived nuclear waste**.

cards.front_md: Give three advantages of fusion reactors over fission reactors.
cards.back_md: Fusion generates **more energy** than fission per kilogram of fuel, the fuel (hydrogen isotopes from water) is **more abundant** than uranium or plutonium, and fusion produces **no long-lived nuclear waste**.

front_blocks.md: Compared with fission reactors, the conditions required for nuclear fusion are much **______** to achieve and maintain on Earth.

back_blocks.md: Compared with fission reactors, the conditions required for nuclear fusion are much **harder** to achieve and maintain on Earth.

cards.front_md: Compared with fission reactors, the conditions required for nuclear fusion are much **______** to achieve and maintain on Earth.
cards.back_md: Compared with fission reactors, the conditions required for nuclear fusion are much **harder** to achieve and maintain on Earth.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Nuclear fusion reactors are currently a commercially viable method of generating electricity.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Fusion reactors are **not yet** commercially viable for generating electricity, although they are in development.

front_blocks.md: Define **nuclear fusion**, as it occurs in stars.

back_blocks.md: In the centre of a star, **hydrogen nuclei** undergo nuclear fusion to form **helium nuclei**, releasing a huge amount of energy.

cards.front_md: Define **nuclear fusion**, as it occurs in stars.
cards.back_md: In the centre of a star, **hydrogen nuclei** undergo nuclear fusion to form **helium nuclei**, releasing a huge amount of energy.

front_blocks.md: Define **electrostatic repulsion**, as it applies to nuclear fusion.

back_blocks.md: The repulsive force between two positively charged **protons**. Nuclei must have very high **kinetic energy** to overcome this repulsion and get close enough to fuse.

cards.front_md: Define **electrostatic repulsion**, as it applies to nuclear fusion.
cards.back_md: The repulsive force between two positively charged **protons**. Nuclei must have very high **kinetic energy** to overcome this repulsion and get close enough to fuse.

front_blocks.md: What prevents a star from collapsing under its own gravity?

back_blocks.md: The heat produced by nuclear fusion provides an outward pressure that balances the inward pull of gravity, keeping the star in **equilibrium**.

cards.front_md: What prevents a star from collapsing under its own gravity?
cards.back_md: The heat produced by nuclear fusion provides an outward pressure that balances the inward pull of gravity, keeping the star in **equilibrium**.

front_blocks.md: What happens in larger stars once the core temperature is hot enough?

back_blocks.md: **Helium nuclei** can fuse together to form heavier elements.

cards.front_md: What happens in larger stars once the core temperature is hot enough?
cards.back_md: **Helium nuclei** can fuse together to form heavier elements.

front_blocks.md: Why are extremely high pressures (densities), in addition to high temperatures, required for nuclear fusion to occur?

back_blocks.md: High densities increase the number of collisions between nuclei, which increases the chance that fusion reactions take place.

cards.front_md: Why are extremely high pressures (densities), in addition to high temperatures, required for nuclear fusion to occur?
cards.back_md: High densities increase the number of collisions between nuclei, which increases the chance that fusion reactions take place.

front_blocks.md: Nuclear fusion requires extremely high **______** and extremely high **______**.

back_blocks.md: Nuclear fusion requires extremely high **temperatures** and extremely high **pressures**.

cards.front_md: Nuclear fusion requires extremely high **______** and extremely high **______**.
cards.back_md: Nuclear fusion requires extremely high **temperatures** and extremely high **pressures**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
On Earth, under normal conditions, fusion reactions between nuclei occur very frequently.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Under normal conditions on Earth, the possibility of collisions between nuclei resulting in fusion is **very low**; the necessary high temperatures and pressures are usually only found in the cores of stars.
